segmenti.tekst: Praise belongs to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala (glorified and exalted is He), and may blessings and peace be upon the Prophet Muhammad, alayhis-salatu was-salam. And after that, first of all, I would like to thank the respected hafiz for the invitation to finally be here with you, so that we can spend these few minutes together with a deed, or through a deed, that has special value with Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala.
To such an extent that the Exalted Creator, tabaraka wa ta'ala, has a group of angels who travel the Earth looking for places where Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is remembered.

And when they find such a place where Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is remembered, they call one another to sit down and listen. And then they listen together with those present, and in the end Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, informs the angels that He has forgiven all who were present. And even if there were no other reward except this reward – to be honored, to come to a place and sit together with the angels and listen – that alone should be enough motivation,

an incentive for each of us to always, or as often as possible, be in places where Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, is remembered. And after that, after thanking the respected hafiz, we also thank the Meshihat of the Islamic Community in Serbia, and the Majlis of Novi Pazar, who made this evening's lecture possible for us. We ask Allah to reward them and all of you with the best reward of this world.

One of the distinguishing qualities of Allah's Messenger Muhammad, especially in relation to his companions, the Sahabah, and in general when it comes to his ummah, his followers, is that the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him), wished them well.
And that the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, cared a great deal about the companions, and he feared that they would live through some difficult moments, some severe trials.

Part of that care of his is the hadith that we will mention this evening. That is, we will, in sha Allah, comment on only one part of it, and on another occasion, if there are more lectures here in Pazar, we will comment on the other parts as well, because each of these things is a story in itself and a lesson in itself, and we fear that if we mentioned all of these things at once and went into detail to a certain extent, it would be too much.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, radiyallahu anhu (may Allah be pleased with him): “Aqbala alayna Rasulullahi, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, fa qal” – on one occasion the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, came and said: “Ya ma'shar al-muhajirin” – O community of Muhajirun (emigrants) – “khamsun idha ubtulitum bihinna, wa a'udhu billahi an tudrikuhunna” –
if you are tested with five things – and I ask Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, or I seek refuge in Allah from that, that is, from your being tested with those five things.

And he says: “Lam tazhar al-fahishatu fi qawmin qattu hatta yu'linu biha…” He says: never has immorality appeared among any people, to the point that they committed it openly – that is, immorality appears publicly – without them being struck by plagues and severe diseases that had not struck the peoples before them.

From this part of this hadith of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam – this is the first thing, there are four more – from this first part of the hadith of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, we understand, among other things, the Prophet's [unclear] care for the companions and his love for the companions, and his supplication to Allah that the companions not live to see certain difficult moments.

From which we understand that everyone who has a certain position of care toward someone, of trust toward someone – the head of a household in relation to his family, an imam in relation to his congregation, a chief imam in relation to his imams, the mufti in relation to the entire Islamic Community, the Reis-ul-ulema when it comes to the Meshihat, and so on – each of them should have this quality that the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, had, and that is care

for those for whom he bears responsibility, and love for them, and fear for the faith of those people, and fear that those people might be struck by a certain trial that they cannot bear, or in which they might, Allah forbid, subhanahu wa ta'ala… And his supplication that those people not live through such moments, and that they not be struck by hard times and severe trials, where it is a question whether the believer will overcome that trial or not.

From this we also understand that sins have their consequences. Every sin has its consequence. And both the individual and the community should know this. A person cannot sin on an individual level without expecting the consequence of that sinning.

Every sin has its consequence, and here the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, mentions certain sins and mentions their consequences. And this is inevitable when it comes to sinning, that is, the consequences of sinning. And that is why the believer should be aware of it.

Whenever you sin against Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, you should know that it has a consequence. One of those consequences is here, this sin that the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, mentions, when it comes to the appearance of immorality, that is, the public commission of immorality.

And every other sin as well. That is why the believer should guard himself against sins. And he must not neglect any sin. And he must not belittle sins, saying: “This sin is small, it has no real consequences. This sin is only this big, it has no real consequences.” All sins have consequences.

Even if sin had no other consequence except that it is the reason why, every time you sin, a black spot appears on your heart, that would be calamity enough for you – that the most important organ in your body becomes stained, on which all your other deeds depend, on which your tongue and what you say depend, and on which your actions and what you do depend. That is why the believing man and the believing woman should be careful when it comes to sinning, that is, not to look at sins – small and great – the way, unfortunately, is the case today.

And when a person asks about a sin, he asks: is it small or great? When he asks about some command of the Prophet, alayhis-salatu was-salam, he asks: is it obligatory or not? At what level is that command? That is not recorded among the first generations. That is not recorded among the first generations of Muslims.

That the Prophet, alayhis-salatu was-salam, would command something, and someone would come and say: “Is it obligatory? Or is it a command of some lesser level?” – that did not exist. Or when it comes to prohibitions – that did not exist. Rather, the Prophet [unclear] commanded something – and it was carried out.

And they did not ask whether it was a command of this level or a command of that level; rather, it was carried out. Unlike people, Muslims who live in the time of today, in which we live: “Is it obligatory? Is it a strict command? Is it a strict prohibition?

Is it a minor sin? Is it a major sin?” That is not asked. Commanded – it is carried out. Forbidden – you abandon it. If you want to follow the earlier generations and live the way they lived. So, sins have their consequences.

And here the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, mentions sins and their consequences. And he mentions here the first sin. He says: never has immorality appeared openly among any people without that people being struck by plagues and severe diseases that were unknown to those before them.
From this we understand how great the danger is when immorality spreads, that is, indecency, and when it is committed publicly. How can it happen that indecency is committed publicly?

It can happen when in a society there are no people who command good and forbid evil. In a society that has people who command good and forbid evil, it cannot happen that immorality is committed publicly.

And then, as soon as that happens, that immorality is committed publicly, it means that those people, the salihun, the righteous people, if there are any in that place, are not commanding good and forbidding evil, but are letting the situation unfold the way it unfolds.

And then the comments are: “That's his business, that's her business, that's not our business. Why should I care about that? Let it be, she has her parents. Leave him alone, he has his father, there's someone to take care of him, there's this one, there's that one,” and everyone goes his own way.

And then immorality is committed publicly. From which we understand one enormous benefit, which is a postulate, a foundation in the religion: that a society that wants to save itself from Allah's general punishment must have among itself those who command good and forbid evil.

Woe to a community that has no people who command good and forbid evil. And for that reason no one has the right to be angry. A child has no right to be angry at his father and mother who command him to good and forbid him from evil.

That is their obligation. Your father cannot let you sin. Your mother cannot let you sin. Your father cannot let you not pray. Your father cannot let you miss prayers. A mother cannot let you go out onto the street undressed without reacting.

She must react. She must call you to good, she must turn you away from evil, and the child has no right to resent it and to be angry with his parents, and to be bored by it and say “why”; rather, he should understand that it is the obligation of the one to whom Allah has given those children as a trust: to call them to good and turn them away from evil. And they have no right to be angry with their parents, and family members – in the wider and narrower sense – whom someone calls have no right to be angry. He calls them to good and turns them away from evil,

he calls them to perform the prayer, he calls them to be moral, if it is women, and men as well. Because there is immorality on both sides. There is immorality among both. Do not be angry. It is the obligation of the believer to call to good and forbid evil,

as much as he can, each of us. “Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand” – if he is able – “fa in lam yastati' fa bi lisanihi” – if he cannot, then with his tongue. If you cannot with your hand, then with your tongue. And no one can forbid you that. And not only can no one forbid you, but you must do it. When there is evil, you must condemn it, whether someone likes it or not, whether someone loves it or not – that is his problem. Whether it was done by your father, by your paternal uncle, by your mother, by your son,

by this one or that one, in this position or that position – it is irrelevant. These are divine rulings. “Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand” – these are the words of the Prophet, alayhis-salam. Addressed to everyone.

Addressed to everyone. Whoever sees evil, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot… with his tongue; if you cannot with your hand – and of course, there are rules for how evil is removed by hand – if you cannot with your hand, then with your tongue. Perhaps you say, perhaps you speak up: “People, this is not good, people, this is wrong, what is happening is not good at all.” No one has the right to deny you that, that freedom, and do not let anyone deny it to you.

Whether you dare to say “a”, whether you dare to condemn something… so that he does not put you in the option, in the position where you don't dare to say “a”. Anything can happen, anyone can do whatever he wants, I don't dare to say “a”, he doesn't dare to say “a”.

What sense does it make? What sense is there to life, what sense to truth, what sense to anything, what sense to your being a believer, if you don't dare to condemn evil? Of course, you don't use harsh words, you don't use insulting words, but you say: “This is wrong, this is not good, people, this does not lead to good, this does not lead to what is khayr (good), neither for me as an individual, nor for you, nor for the community, wider and narrower.”

The believer must understand, he must understand that every individual has this obligation. If you cannot with your hand, then with your tongue; if you cannot with your tongue – and that can happen, that someone cannot with his tongue – let him condemn it with his heart, and that is the weakest form of iman (faith).

And how then can a person not condemn even with his heart? He sees evil, he has no strength to condemn it with his heart. He sees evil, he won't condemn it because that evil is being done by someone over there with whom he is on some good terms.

So he won't condemn it. [unclear], you don't have the strength to say it – OK, you have an excuse for that. No one will interfere with you, whether you have one or not, you judge that. But at least the heart must work. The heart must condemn evil.

You must not allow your heart to look at evil and to hear about evil without you having a position. You must have a position. From the beginning of the Revelation, from the first day, from the first day, from the first verse, “Iqra'”, until the last moment of the Prophet and his companions, truth and falsehood were distinguished.

And the followers of the truth had a position. The follower of the truth had a position. He had a position regarding the disorder of that time, in that era. And he knew what was haqq (truth) and what was batil (falsehood). And he stood on the side of the truth and spoke against falsehood and what was false.
And that from the first days – read Surah Al-Alaq. In the first verses that were revealed, Allah speaks about this. He speaks about those who are on the side of falsehood.

Why does Allah speak about Abu Jahl and how he prevented people from prayer, from worship, from obedience to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, at the very beginning? So that you know, you who have accepted Islam today – today you accepted Islam – you should know that in Islam there is something called awliya' ar-Rahman and awliya' ash-shaytan: the allies of Allah and the allies of Satan. And that lasts until the Day of Judgment, and it cannot be otherwise, and there is no other Islam, and there exists no other Islam, and there is no other straight path, there exists no other straight path, there is no straight path without this.

There is no straight path without it. I cannot walk the straight path without anyone ever saying [unclear] to me, without anyone ever calling me out, without anyone ever saying an ugly word to me. That is impossible, that has never existed. The best of men, Allah's Messenger, lived – he was born among that people and lived among them.

The Trustworthy, al-Amin, and the Truthful – that was his nickname. That was his nickname. No stain on his character. Never. And that is how his people knew him. However, when it came to standing with the truth and defending the truth, calling to it, and thereby pointing out that everything contrary to it is a lie, then those closest to him accused him of lying.

And they said that he was a liar, and a poet, and a sorcerer, and that he separated a father from his son and a brother [unclear]. And that is the nature of the straight path. That is why the person who is on the straight path, the Muslim man and Muslim woman, should know that this is one of the rules, of the divine sunnah (way) of the straight path.

And you will not find a single prophet, a single prophet who called to the Straight Path, without there being, on the other side, enemies of the truth who invented various words and slanders. That does not exist. Such a one does not exist. They all had those kinds of trials. Why?

Because that is the nature of the straight path. And do not think that you can belong to some religion and be on some manhaj. He says: “I am on the manhaj, I am on the Sunnah.” What does manhaj mean for you? What is the Sunnah for you? That everything is burning, that the land is burning, and you have no position; that the land is burning and you don't dare to say “a” – is that it? Is that the religion? Is that the follower of the truth? Is that the pride? What is that?

That is why the believer should know what the nature of the straight path is. This does not mean that the believer should not be careful about what he says, saying: “I am upon the truth,” and then blurting things out, doing all sorts of things, not being careful about his deeds – we are not talking about that. The believer must weigh everything, examine it, and put it within the framework of the Shari'ah.

But he should be aware of this: that there must be people in society who will call to good and forbid evil. Otherwise indecency appears, which, when it is committed publicly, brings upon people what the Prophet, alayhis-salam, mentioned.

Why? There are no people who call to good and forbid evil. And that is why no one has the right to resent those who call to good and forbid evil. A child should not resent his parents. A congregation should not resent its imams.

They bring an imam, they employ an imam. The imam teaches the religion, and then half the congregation is smarter than the imam. Take the robe, barakallahu fik (may Allah bless you), be the imam. Don't pay imams for nothing. When there are so many imams, each of you take a robe and take turns every day.

When the time for Jumu'ah comes, let each of you put on a robe and – go ahead, onto the minbar. You're paying imams for nothing, you're putting yourselves to expense. But if you have brought a man to teach you – even though he is an imam, even though he warns you about evil and tells you what is good, that is his obligation – you should come and kiss him on the forehead and say: “May Allah reward you for calling us to good, for pointing out to us what is wrong, for warning us. Maybe I don't see it, maybe I haven't seen it, I didn't know these things. May Allah reward you.”

But here you are looking for someone who will stroke you the right way nonstop: “Is this allowed?” “It is.” “Is this allowed?” “It is.” “Is this allowed?” “It is.” Just so as not to offend you. Rather, you should value such a man. You should not resent him.
Imams should not be resented when they say certain things and criticize certain social phenomena. They should not be resented. An imam is an imam. He should be one in the true sense of the word.

And no one has the right to resent him if he is right; if he is not, even an imam can be told: “Forgive me, you are not right.” But if he is right, there is no resentment. You're my imam as long as you keep quiet and I do whatever I want; as soon as you say “a”, then you are no longer my imam, you are no longer my authority. There is no blame on them, it is their obligation.

Whenever we see something, walking around the town, listening, [unclear] we give a lesson. Because we know that it is some social deviation that we should point out. Sometimes it is indecency, sometimes it is bribery and corruption, sometimes it is something else, sometimes something third.

Sometimes it concerns the city, sometimes it concerns an individual, sometimes it concerns some phenomenon – whatever it is doesn't matter. And that was the work of Allah's messengers, alayhimus-salam. Every messenger was sent to a certain people and treated the social problems that were occurring.

What kind of messenger would it be – a certain deviation appears among his people, and he stays silent? In the time of Lut, Allah's messenger, that moral deviation appeared – and what, should he now stay silent because it appeared among the people? It is his obligation to treat it. In the time of other messengers of Allah there were other deviations, other sins, and that is why Allah mentioned in the Qur'an those messengers and the deviations: the messenger, the deviation and the treatment, his struggle against it, throughout the whole time of his mission.

That is a completely normal thing. And it is not normal to demand something else from the learned. And no one can demand something else from the learned; rather, it is their obligation. If the imam on the minbar does not warn me and you, who listen to him, about something, does not call us to something that is good, who will call us in this world of rushing, busyness, calamities and everything that is happening around us?

Who will call you? Where will you hear anything, if the imam doesn't do it? It is the obligation of imams. Imams should do this. Imams should be respected for this. And they should be valued. And what imams say, advise and warn about should be taken into account.

Whoever is able to take it into account: when imams speak about this and that, how it is not good – let's do something about it. There is indecency – let's see what we can do; there is disorder – let's see; there is corruption – let's see what we can do. And not then the talk: “What does he have to say about that, that's not his business, it's not this, it's not…” Fine, then what is his business? What is his business? What is his business?

If the main deviations among the people are not treated, what should the imam come out and talk about? And what should he talk about? That is why, as need demands and according to what is happening in society, the imam positions himself that way and speaks about those things. That is why no one has the right to resent him,

neither the congregation, when it comes to his mosque, his community in the narrower sense, nor in the wider sense; rather, his role is to speak the truth. And you who have a certain trust, which you carry on your back – you took it on, you took it on yourself, did anyone force you to take it? No one forced you, you even imposed yourself on people [unclear]. You took on the trust, go ahead: we will praise you when you do something good, and criticize you when you do something bad, and you too have the same right,

when it comes to someone else, to do… And don't expect someone to sing your praises here; rather, understand that it is the obligation of people to call to good and forbid evil. Otherwise, if there are none who call to good and forbid evil, that has its… that has its consequences. And it is not enough for a person to be good.
And here there is one great delusion, and that is that a person prays, worships Allah, fasts, and so on. He is good, salih. A salih man, good. But he is not muslih. He does not set anything right.

[unclear]. Everything can collapse. Everything can be set on fire. I don't care at all. Let everyone do whatever he wants. It is not enough only to worship Allah; rather, when it comes to these things, you must be an integral part of it and set things right.
Otherwise, when Allah's punishment comes because of sins, it encompasses both the sinners and those who were good – basically those who were good – but did not call to good and forbid evil.

Thus it is narrated from Zaynab bint Jahsh that she once said to Allah's Messenger, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam: “A nahliku wa fina as-salihun?” She said: “Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?” And the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, said: “Na'am, idha kathura al-khabath.”

“Yes, if corruption, sinning and disobedience spread.” The fact that there are good people among you is not a reason for Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, not to punish that community. He said: “Yes, if corruption spreads.” And that is why it is not normal, it is not normal that there is a good servant of Allah, basically obedient to Allah, while around him corruption spreads and he does not react to it and [unclear] it.

And that is why these are extremely important things that we need to understand, especially we here. Because here among us, our people are specific. Unfortunately, they have one peculiarity that is negative, and that is that whoever they sit with, they are of his opinion.

You cannot find two men who will sit together, who have opposing opinions on the question of [unclear], and who will talk and argue: I advocate one thing, and you advocate another. Either they will come to blows if they disagree, or they will [unclear]: “Uh-huh, yes, yes, yes.”

While he sits with him – it's all “yes”. “Is this one good?” “Yes.” “Is that one good?” “Yes.” “Is the fifth one good?” “Yes.” They are all… As soon as he leaves that man: “Did you see this fool, did you see this one, this one is like this, she is like that, she is like that.”

[unclear]. Why do you allow yourself that? Why do you allow yourself to live like that? That is a fall, that is a spiritual fall, to live like a slave, to live like a slave, not daring to tell a man that you don't agree with him. You will notice it in communication: as soon as you start to disagree with a person, he senses it – hop, immediately he backs down: “Yes, uh-huh, uh-huh” – hop, hop… another 30 seconds and the conversation is over. [unclear]. That is not good, that is not good; rather, a person must have his own position, and if he disagrees with someone, in the nicest possible way, and back up what he holds with arguments.
And look at the world that way. You view all events that way. You view everything through argumentation. You see a certain phenomenon – you analyze it with arguments, either positively or negatively.

You see someone doing something – you analyze it with arguments. You want to evaluate a person – you evaluate them with arguments. And then you know exactly what you need to do. If you need to decide on something, on some opinion, on some person, and to support someone, you know exactly what you need to do.

However, when a person lacks these abilities, or when he lives a life of “it's all good, it's all the same, it's all… it's all… that”, then what happens happens. Also, in this sense, it is narrated that the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, said: “Inna an-nasa idha ra'aw al-munkar” – he said: when people see munkar, that which is evil – “fa lam yughayyiruhu” – and do not change it at all, they see evil and do not change that evil,

they leave it as it is – he said: “awshaka an ya'ummahumullahu bi 'iqabihi” – it is to be feared that Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, will punish them all. When people see some evil and do not change it, it is to be feared that Allah will punish them all,

both those who do the evil and those who do not do that evil but watch it. That is why this is a foundation, a foundation of our religion. And it is impossible to live on this Earth, if a person wants to live correctly, within the framework of Islam, without this principle:

commanding good and forbidding evil. If a person sees evil and does not react and lets it be, then we come to a situation where that evil is committed publicly. And then, when that evil is committed publicly, it becomes normalized, and it is very hard for a person to do anything after that.

That is why these words of the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, should be a lesson. Every sin has its consequence. That is why one should react to evil, so that it does not happen that because of that evil Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, sends certain punishments to a people, and that after that the best of that people supplicate to Allah, and Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, does not answer their supplications.

Rather, the believer should do what is up to him: to understand what the straight path is, to know what the truth is, to know what falsehood is, to know that he should stand with the truth, to know that he must be against falsehood.

Just imagine what it was like for the earlier generations, what it was like for the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, what it was like for him in that society in which the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, grew up, what it was like for him with his paternal uncles who cared for him, what it was like for him to stand on the side of truth while they stood on the side of falsehood, and to carry that truth with pride.

Do you think that was easy? And our kinds of trials in this sense are much smaller. Our kinds of trials in this sense are much smaller. Back then it meant an enormous sacrifice. Back then it sometimes led to a situation where in some battles a man had to stand against his closest relative:

he on one side, the other on the other side, and both carrying swords; this one upon truth, that one upon falsehood. And holding fast to the straight path sometimes meant that too. And you know, and you have probably heard, the event connected with the well-known munafiq (hypocrite) from the time of the Prophet, alayhis-salam.

When news spread that, because he was a hypocrite and a munafiq, the Muslims were saying that he should be wiped off the Earth, that someone should eliminate him for it. His son Abdullah heard this, and he came to the Prophet, alayhis-salam.

He said: “O Messenger of Allah, I have heard what people are saying about my father” – and his father was the leader of the hypocrites – “I have heard what people are saying about my father, this father of mine,” and he said: “I could not bear for the killer of my father to walk the Earth.
That would be hard. I cannot bear it,” he said. “So allow me to do it. If it has to happen, if he must be eliminated, then allow me to do it.”

Then he came to the entrance of Medina – they were returning from some campaign, and Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, revealed verses of the Qur'an. The hypocrites had been talking among themselves: when we return to Medina, the mighty will expel the weak – that is, they, that group of hypocrites, would expel the Prophet, alayhis-salam, and the believers from Medina – and Allah revealed that in those Qur'anic verses.

So he stood at the entrance of Medina and, when his father came by, he said: “As for you, you cannot come in. As for you, you cannot come in until the Prophet, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, permits you to enter.”

Then the Prophet, alayhis-salam, permitted him, and he entered – he let him enter Medina. Imagine that kind of trial, imagine that manner of trial, to be tested in that way. And that is why the biography of the Prophet, everything related to the biography – the whole of Islam is there. Everything is there.

The whole of Islam is there. And that is why the one who listens to and reads about the biography of the Prophet, alayhis-salam, should try to live those moments. Not to read it and retell it, but to try to live that moment: if you were in that situation, how would you act?

If you were on one side and your father on the other, and your father is what he is, and then someone has to deal with him. How would a person act in that situation, and how many calculators would he pull out to calculate, to see how and what, what if this, what if that, what…

And in this, among other things, lies one of the essential differences between us and the earlier generations: when they accepted the truth, that was it. No more left and right. Unlike the hypocrites, who have one story for one chair, for one gathering, another story for another gathering, a third story for a third gathering.

So, from this first thing in this hadith of the Prophet, alayhis-salam, we understand the Prophet's care, alayhis-salam, for his companions, his love for them, his concern that they not fall into something, his fear for them, that there not come a time of immorality and catastrophe that they might live through.

And here he addresses the Muhajirun, he says: “O community of Muhajirun.” Why does he address the Muhajirun? It is said that it is because the Muhajirun suffered a great deal for the sake of da'wah and went through various kinds of trials back then, at that time, so he addresses them specifically in this hadith; however, it encompasses all other Muslims.

And we also understand that sins have their consequences, that the believer must guard himself against sins, and we also understand that in societies there must be those who call to good and forbid evil, and that it is not enough for a person to be, in himself, obedient only to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, but that he must react to evil.

And we mentioned the ways of reacting when it comes to evil, and that is that a person changes it with his hand if he can; if he cannot, with his tongue; if he cannot, then condemns it with his heart, and that is the weakest form of iman. Here there are, as we said, four more things that are also important.

If there is some opportunity here in Pazar for another lecture, in sha Allah, in sha Allah, as far as we manage, we will mention each of those things and comment on them.
